chunks: From him, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad al-A'lawi, from al-Amraki, from Safwan, from Ali ibn Matar, from Abdullah ibn Sinan, who said:

I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: 'Two men disputed over a beast of burden and went to Ali (peace be upon him). Each claimed it had given birth at his place, on his milking stand, and both presented evidence equal in number. He cast lots between them with two lots, marking each lot with a sign for each of them, then said: "O God, Lord of the seven heavens and Lord of the seven earths and Lord of the Great Throne, Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, the Merciful, the Compassionate, which of them is the owner of the beast and has the stronger claim to it? I ask You to reveal and bring forth his lot." The lot of one of them came out, so he ruled in his favor. And also, when two disputants quarreled over a slave girl, one claimed he bought her and the other claimed she was born to him, if they both presented evidence, he ruled in favor of the one to whom she was born.'
ai.seo_question: How did Imam Ali resolve property disputes when both parties presented equal evidence?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* illustrates Imam Ali’s (peace be upon him) pragmatic judicial methodology, specifically the use of *al-qar’* (casting lots) as a mechanism for divine selection (*kashf*) when evidentiary proofs are perfectly balanced. The ruling prioritizing birth (*intaj*) over purchase in the second case reflects the Shia scholarly understanding that possession derived from natural generation carries a stronger presumptive claim (*istishab*) than mere transactional acquisition when other indicators are equal.
